question: Which of these is the main organ responsible for our sense of touch?
explanation: You've got this! The skin is the body's largest organ and is packed with special nerve endings that help us feel the world around us. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T11#GNS211_U4_T11_h1)

question: When we talk about 'somatosensation', what kind of feelings are we including?
explanation: Great try! Somatosensation covers all the general body feelings like touch, temperature, pain, and knowing where your limbs are. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T11#GNS211_U4_T11_h1)

question: Which type of sensory receptor specifically picks up physical changes like pressure and vibration?
explanation: Think of 'mechano' as movement! Mechanoreceptors are the clever nerve endings that convert physical touch and pressure into signals your brain understands. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T11#GNS211_U4_T11_h2)

question: What is special about the mechanoreceptors sitting right near the surface of the skin?

options.B: They have small receptive fields for fine detail
options.C: They respond exclusively to extreme temperatures
options.D: They only detect deep, heavy pressure

explanation: Spot on! Because their receptive fields are small, superficial receptors help your brain pinpoint exact touches and feel fine textures. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T11#GNS211_U4_T11_h2)

question: Which touch receptors deep in the skin are best at detecting heavy pressure and fast vibrations?
explanation: You can do this! Pacinian corpuscles sit deep down and are fine-tuned to catch sudden vibrations and deep pressure changes. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T11#GNS211_U4_T11_h3)

question: A patient runs their fingers over rough fabric to feel the texture. Which skin receptor is working hardest here?
explanation: Well done! Merkel disks are close to the surface and give your brain wonderful, detailed feedback about shapes, edges, and rough textures. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T11#GNS211_U4_T11_h3)

question: What actually opens the ion channels on a touch receptor when you press on the skin?

options.A: Physical stretching of the cell membrane
options.C: A drop in core body temperature

explanation: Think of it like a tiny trapdoor: when you press on the skin, the physical stretch pulls the cell membrane open so ions can flow through! [learn more](GNS211_U4_T11#GNS211_U4_T11_h4)

question: What happens right after positive ions rush into a touch receptor during a physical push?

options.D: Blood flow to the skin stops completely

explanation: You're getting the hang of it! That rush of positive ions changes the electrical charge inside, creating a small spark (receptor potential) that fires off a message. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T11#GNS211_U4_T11_h4)

question: Which nerve pathway carries fine touch and vibration signals all the way up to the brain?
explanation: Don't let the long name scare you! The dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway is just the main highway for detailed touch and vibration. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T11#GNS211_U4_T11_h5)

question: Where do the nerve fibers in the dorsal column pathway cross over to the opposite side of the body?
explanation: Spot on! As these sensory messages travel up, they cross over to the other side once they reach the lower part of the brainstem called the medulla. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T11#GNS211_U4_T11_h5)

question: In which lobe of the brain is the primary touch (somatosensory) cortex found?
explanation: You've got this! The parietal lobe sits right at the top-back of your brain and is the main station for processing everything you touch. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T11#GNS211_U4_T11_h6)

question: Why do our hands and lips take up so much more space in the brain's sensory map than our back?

options.A: They have thicker layers of subcutaneous fat
options.B: They are located closer to the brain
options.C: They receive a larger volume of arterial blood
options.D: They possess a much higher density of touch receptors

explanation: Makes sense, right? We use our hands and lips for detailed tasks, so they need way more brain power and receptor coverage than our backs! [learn more](GNS211_U4_T11#GNS211_U4_T11_h6)

question: Why do nurses ask patients to close their eyes during a simple touch sensation check?

options.A: To stop the pupils from reacting to bright light
options.B: To help the patient relax their heart rate
options.C: To prevent visual cues from replacing or biasing touch feedback
options.D: To prevent dizziness caused by looking around the room

explanation: Smart nursing practice! Closing the eyes makes sure we are strictly testing the patient's nerves and feeling, not letting their eyes do the guessing. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T11#GNS211_U4_T11_h7)

question: A patient with long-term diabetes says they are losing feeling in their feet. How does this nerve loss typically spread?

options.A: Sensory loss appears first in the scalp and face
options.B: Sensory loss affects only one random patch of skin
options.C: Sensory loss starts in the distal toes and moves upward
options.D: Sensory loss starts in the upper chest and moves down

explanation: You're building great clinical intuition! Diabetic neuropathy usually follows a 'stocking-glove' pattern, hitting the longest nerves in the toes first and creeping up. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T11#GNS211_U4_T11_h7)
